summary: This memo gives information that may be useful when choosing a method to assign unique identifiers to people, and discusses how unique such identifiers really are. It is informational.

eli5.summary: How do you give every person a name tag that nobody else has? This paper talks about ways to do that and whether the tags are truly one of a kind.

questions: how to assign unique identifiers to people
subtitle: Making sure every person's account name is truly unique.

tldr.problem: Computer systems need to assign unique identifiers to users, typically as short alphanumeric strings like usernames. However, the method chosen affects both how easily identifiers can be guessed from a person's name and how likely duplicate collisions become.
tldr.mechanism: Identifiers can be generated randomly (no connection to the user's name), derived from the user's name algorithmically (like first and last name combined), or derived from names with collisions handled ad-hoc. Each approach trades predictability against uniqueness and collision likelihood.
tldr.outcome: As email became widespread, name-based identifiers became preferred because people could guess them. However, this increases collision risk significantly, and the RFC provides mathematical analysis of duplicate probabilities across different naming schemes and organization sizes.

today: RFC 1439 remains informational. While email systems have evolved and many organizations now use UUID or other technical identifiers internally, the tension between human-readable, guessable identifiers and uniqueness remains. The privacy concern about identifier reuse is still relevant in systems where usernames are reissued.

sections.title: The Problem of Unique User Identifiers
sections.content:
Computer systems require a way to identify people using them. These identifiers are typically short, alphanumeric strings called usernames or account names, and they must be unique within a system or organization. The RFC addresses a practical challenge: how to assign these identifiers reliably, and what happens when two people end up with the same identifier or similar ones.

With the rise of electronic mail, an important new requirement emerged: the ability to predict an identifier from a person's name. Without this, a user sending email had no way to guess a recipient's address. This pressure to make identifiers predictable conflicts with the goal of ensuring they remain unique.
sections.eli5: Every person needs a login name that is different from everyone else's. The tricky part is: should these names be random (like ax54tv) or based on a person's real name (like craig.finseth)? With real names, people can guess the email address, but then you get two Craigs with the same name.

sections.title: Three Methods for Assigning Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three approaches to assigning unique identifiers. The first method generates identifiers without any connection to the user's identity—examples like ax54tv or cs00034 were common in large timesharing systems. This ensures uniqueness and prevents guessing, but requires users to learn and remember arbitrary strings.

The second method derives identifiers algorithmically from a person's name while ensuring uniqueness, such as Craig.A.Finseth-1, Finseth1, or caf-1. This makes identifiers guessable but requires appending a suffix (often a number) when collisions occur. The third method simply derives the identifier from the name without enforcing uniqueness in the identifier itself—like Craig.Finseth or caf—and handles duplicates through external means or by maintaining a list of aliases.
sections.eli5: You can assign names randomly (nobody can guess them), use a person's name but add a number if two people match (craig.finseth-1), or just use their name and deal with conflicts when they happen.

sections.title: Identifier Formats and Information Content
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs popular identifier formats and analyzes their information-theoretic capacity. Formats using initials have the least information content: single initials have roughly 4 to 5 bits of capacity, while three initials (first, middle, last) have about 12 to 15 bits. Formats using names are richer: a first name alone has 8 to 14 bits, a last name has 9 to 13 bits, and both first and last names together provide 17 to 27 bits of capacity.

Combinations like first initial and full last name provide 13 to 18 bits, while first name with middle initial and last name provide 21 to 32 bits. The RFC presents a complete matrix of combinations, noting that most practical identifier formats contain between 8 and 20 bits of information content. This capacity directly determines how many unique identifiers can exist before collisions become likely.
sections.eli5: Different naming styles carry different amounts of information. Using just one initial (J) can make about 4 different names. Using a full first and last name (John Doe) can make thousands. The more information you include, the less likely two people get the same identifier.

sections.title: Probability of Collisions
sections.content:
The RFC applies the mathematics of the birthday problem to compute collision probabilities for identifier schemes. In an organization of N people, the probability that at least two share an identifier depends on the information content of the identifier format. The RFC provides a table showing thresholds: for a given identifier space (measured in bits), how many people can be added before reaching 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, or 20% probability of a duplicate.

For example, a format with 17 bits of capacity (like first and last name) can accommodate about 52 people before a 1% chance of collision, but with 100 people the probability rises to between 2% and 5%, and with 1,000 people it exceeds 20%. The RFC includes a Perl program and its output to show these calculations across different bit widths, from 6 bits (universe of 64 identifiers) to 31 bits (universe of 2.1 billion identifiers).
sections.eli5: The more people you have, the more likely two end up with the same name. The math (called the birthday problem) can predict exactly when this happens. If you use first and last names (17 bits), you can have about 50 people before you're likely to get a duplicate.

sections.title: Privacy and the Reuse Question
sections.content:
The RFC's appendix raises a subtle but important privacy issue. When an organization reuses identifiers after a person leaves, future users might accidentally receive email intended for the previous holder. For example, if Craig.A.Finseth leaves and another Craig A. Finseth joins, the new person might receive sensitive communications meant for the first.

The RFC references the Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1987, noting that because identifiers are predictable from names, a sender has no reliable way to know if they are reaching the intended person. The solution is to ensure identifiers include a unique suffix (like Craig.A.Finseth-1) and never reuse the plain form—this signals to senders that they must obtain and use the complete, suffixed identifier rather than guessing. This prevents accidental misdirection of email to new people with the same name.
sections.eli5: If someone leaves your company and you give their login to a new person with the same name, emails meant for the old person might go to the new one. Using numbered suffixes makes it clear that names alone are not enough—people need the number too.
